python-q1.testing: whether you know the GIL protects the interpreter, not your code, and can predict when threads help.
python-q1.trap: "the GIL makes Python single-threaded," or its opposite, "the GIL makes my code thread-safe."
python-q1.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "The GIL protects the interpreter's own state, not my data. It's one lock per interpreter that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time."
2 · What CPython does "It exists because every object carries a reference count that changes on almost every operation, and the allocator is shared too. One big lock makes that safe. A thread gives the lock up when it blocks on I/O, when a C extension releases it, or after five milliseconds if another thread is waiting."
3 · Prove it "So it stops mattering in two cases. I/O: twenty threads each sleeping point-two seconds finish in about point-two seconds. And C extensions like NumPy and PyTorch, which release it during heavy work. The victim is CPU-bound pure Python: four threads take about as long as one."
4 · Where it bites in production "Two consequences. It doesn't make my code thread-safe: counter plus-equals one is several bytecodes, so I still need locks. And one CPU-heavy thread in a web worker adds latency to every other request."
5 · What changes by version "Python 3.12 allows one GIL per sub-interpreter, and 3.13 ships an optional free-threaded build without it."
Close "It guards the interpreter; I/O and C code step around it; pure-Python CPU work doesn't."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"The GIL makes CPython's internals safe to use from several threads. It says nothing about the safety of my own data structures."

The GIL protects The GIL does not protect
reference counts on every object counter += 1 on a shared variable
the memory allocator check-then-act on a dict (if k not in d: d[k] = …)
internal structures during a dict resize or list growth any invariant that spans two statements
Register Fact
CPython detail the GIL itself; PyPy has one too; Jython and IronPython never did; 3.13t can run without it
Scope one GIL per interpreter; a thread must hold it to execute Python bytecode

stages.name: What CPython does
stages.claim: refcounts, a token, a 5 ms hand-off
stages.html:
"Think of it as a token that threads pass around."

Time Thread A (CPU work) Thread B (I/O) Holds the GIL
0 ms runs bytecode waiting on a socket (released the GIL) A
2 ms runs bytecode data arrives; wants the GIL A
7 ms asked to drop it after the 5 ms switch interval acquires it, runs its Python code B
8 ms waiting blocks on the next read: releases A
The GIL changes hands when Detail
a thread blocks on I/O socket, file, time.sleep → it releases the GIL
a C extension releases it around heavy work (Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS)
another thread has waited for the switch interval sys.getswitchinterval() → 0.005 s by default
Work type Do threads run in parallel?
Waiting on network / disk waits overlap
NumPy / torch / hashlib on large buffers mostly, GIL released in C
Pure-Python loops, parsing, JSON in Python one thread at a time

Why it exists: one big lock made refcounting and the allocator safe without per-object locking, and kept single-threaded code fast.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: scaling, and a race it doesn't stop
stages.html:
"Run it and look at the shape: CPU-bound threads don't speed up, sleeping ones do."

Workload 1 thread 4 threads Reading
cpu (pure Python) t ≈ 4 t no speed-up: one thread at a time
io (sleep) 0.5 s ≈ 0.5 s 4× the throughput: waits overlap 
import threading, time
def cpu():  sum(i * i for i in range(3_000_000))    # pure Python bytecode
def io():   time.sleep(0.5)                          # releases the GIL while waiting
def run(fn, k):
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=fn) for _ in range(k)]
    t = time.perf_counter(); [x.start() for x in ts]; [x.join() for x in ts]
    return time.perf_counter() - t
for fn in (cpu, io):
    print(fn.__name__, f"{run(fn, 1):.2f}s vs 4 threads {run(fn, 4):.2f}s")
# → expect: cpu ≈ 4× the single-thread time (no speedup); io ≈ the same 0.5 s (4× throughput)

And why the GIL isn't thread safety: += on a shared value is several bytecodes.

import dis
x = 0
def bump():
    global x
    x += 1
dis.dis(bump)
# → LOAD_GLOBAL x · LOAD_CONST 1 · BINARY_OP (+=) · STORE_GLOBAL x   (3.12; names vary by version)

LOAD_GLOBAL x        ← read
LOAD_CONST 1
BINARY_OP +=         ← modify       a thread switch here loses an update
STORE_GLOBAL x       ← write

Use a threading.Lock, a queue.Queue, or avoid shared mutable state.

stages.name: Where it bites in production
stages.claim: CPU work in an I/O service
stages.html:
"The GIL rarely limits throughput of an I/O service. It hurts latency when CPU work sneaks into it."

Situation What happens Fix
FastAPI endpoint runs tokenisation / JSON-heavy parsing in a thread pool other requests wait on the GIL; p99 rises move CPU work to a ProcessPoolExecutor or a separate worker service
Background thread doing Python computation in a web worker convoy effect: I/O threads wake up and wait for the GIL offload to processes; keep web workers I/O-only
Embedding pipeline calling a model via torch fine with threads; the heavy work is in C/GPU threads or async are OK; watch data loading in Python
CPU-bound batch job threads give no speed-up multiprocessing / process pool, or vectorise with NumPy
See it with Shows
py-spy dump --pid <pid> which thread holds the GIL, and where
py-spy top hot Python frames
asyncio debug mode slow callbacks on the loop

stages.name: What changes by version
stages.html:
"The GIL is becoming optional, one step at a time."

Version Change Note
3.12 per-interpreter GIL (PEP 684) sub-interpreters can run Python in parallel in one process (limited API)
3.13 optional free-threaded build (PEP 703, python3.13t) no GIL, per-object locking and biased refcounting; single-threaded code runs somewhat slower; C extensions must declare support
Senior stance:check wheelscheck the code doesn't lean on the GIL for safetymeasure on a CPU-bound jobadopt where the gain is real

followUps.question: Four threads each run for _ in range(1_000_000): x += 1 on a global. What does print(x) show?
followUps.html:
Something up to 4,000,000, and you must not rely on it being exact.

thread A: LOAD x (41) ─ switch ─────────────────▶ STORE 42
thread B:              LOAD x (41) → STORE 42            ← one update lost

Recent CPython versions make lost updates rarer for this exact loop because of when switches are checked. That's an implementation detail, not a guarantee. Protect it with a Lock.

followUps.question: "So Python can't do multithreading?"
followUps.html:
It can, and does. What it can't do is run Python bytecode on several cores at once.

Threads in standard CPython
Run concurrently and overlap I/O
Run C extensions in parallel (GIL released)
Execute bytecode on several cores at once → processes, or the 3.13 free-threaded build

followUps.question: Why does one CPU-heavy thread slow down the I/O threads?
followUps.html:
Every I/O wake-up has to wait for the CPU thread to give the GIL back.

Convoy:data arrivesthe I/O thread needs the GILthe CPU thread holds itforced hand-offthe I/O thread runs

Many such waits show up as tail latency.

followUps.question: Your FastAPI service's p99 doubled after adding a PDF-parsing step in a sync endpoint. What do you do?
followUps.html:
Confirm it holds the GIL, then move it out of the web worker.

Step Action
Confirm py-spy shows parsing on the hot path, holding the GIL
Move a ProcessPoolExecutor via run_in_executor, or a worker service fed by a queue
Verify p99 and event-loop lag after the change; pool sized to cores

followUps.question: Would you switch production to the free-threaded 3.13t build?
followUps.html:
Not yet as a default. I'd pilot it on a CPU-heavy batch job first.

Check Why
Every C extension ships free-threaded wheels otherwise it won't load, or re-enables the GIL
The code doesn't rely on the GIL for implicit safety hidden races appear
Measured gain single-threaded speed is lower; gains appear only for CPU-bound Python threads

followUps.question: Why do threads calling NumPy scale when pure-Python threads don't?
followUps.html:
NumPy releases the GIL inside its C loops for large arrays.

Workload Scales with threads?
Large arrays, time spent in C
Small arrays, much Python between calls the Python lines still take the GIL

dontSay: "The GIL makes Python single-threaded." — threads run and overlap I/O.
"The GIL makes my code thread-safe." — compound operations still race.
"Python is slow because of the GIL." — most slowness is interpretation overhead, not the lock.
"The GIL is part of the Python language." — it's a CPython implementation detail.

spine: What I'd pick for an AI backend
python-q2.testing: whether you choose by where the time goes, not by taste or fashion.
python-q2.trap: "asyncio is the modern one, so always asyncio," or "threads are useless because of the GIL."
python-q2.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "I pick by asking one question first: where does the time actually go? Waiting, or computing? And if computing, in Python or in C? I measure that before choosing."
2 · Where asyncio wins "If it's waiting on the network or disk and my libraries are async, I use asyncio. One thread and one event loop hold thousands of open sockets, because a coroutine gives up control at every await. That's the shape of an AI backend."
3 · Where threads win "If it's waiting but the library is sync-only, like an old SDK, I use a bounded thread pool. Threads release the GIL while they block. Threads are also fine when the CPU work is inside C, like NumPy or torch."
4 · Where processes win "If it's burning CPU in pure Python bytecode, threads won't help because of the GIL, so I use processes: a process pool or a separate worker service. I pay for pickling and for a copy of memory per process."
5 · What I'd pick for an AI backend "In practice I mix them: an async API, to-thread for the odd sync call, and a process pool or worker tier for heavy Python CPU work."
Close "Waiting goes to asyncio or threads; Python CPU goes to processes; C-level CPU can stay on threads."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: waiting vs computing, and in which language
stages.html:
"The choice isn't about style. It's about whether the time is waiting or computing, and whether the computing is in Python or in C."

Where the time goes Tool Why
Waiting, async library available asyncio one thread, thousands of concurrent waits
Waiting, sync-only library thread pool threads release the GIL while blocked
CPU in Python bytecode processes each process has its own GIL
CPU in C (NumPy, torch) threads the extension releases the GIL
  • Measure first: wall-clock vs CPU time. time.perf_counter() vs time.process_time() on one request tells you which row you're in.

stages.name: Where asyncio wins
stages.html:
asyncio A thread per wait
Cost of one waiter a coroutine: a few KB a stack (MBs of reserved virtual memory) + OS scheduling
Switch points only at await: explicit anywhere: pre-emptive
Requirement every call on the path is async none
One blocking call stalls every request on the loop stalls one thread

See blocking-call-in-async-handler for the last row.

  • A coroutine costs a few KB; a thread costs a stack (MBs of reserved virtual memory) plus OS scheduling.
  • Explicit await points make shared state easier to reason about: no switch can happen between two lines without an await.
  • Cost: everything on the path must be async. One blocking call stalls every request on that loop (see blocking-call-in-async-handler).

Prove it — 100 concurrent waits on one thread:

import asyncio, time, threading
async def call():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)          # stands in for an HTTP call to a model provider
async def main():
    t = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(call() for _ in range(100)))
    print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s", threading.active_count())
asyncio.run(main())
# → 0.5s 1   (100 waits overlap; one thread)

stages.name: Where threads win
stages.html:
"Threads are right in two cases: a blocking library, and CPU work that lives in C."

Case Why threads work Watch for
Sync-only SDK or driver a thread blocked on a socket releases the GIL: 20 threads → 20 overlapping calls an unbounded pool exhausts memory and file descriptors
NumPy, torch, hashlib, tokenizers the C loop releases the GIL: real parallelism, shared memory, no pickling the Python between the calls still takes the GIL
Shared state — pre-emptive switching: x += 1 is not atomic
From async code:await asyncio.to_thread(sync_fn, arg)runs on the loop's default executorthe loop stays free
  • A thread blocked on a socket releases the GIL, so a pool of 20 threads makes 20 sync HTTP calls overlap.
  • NumPy, torch, hashlib and most tokenizers release the GIL inside C loops: threads get real parallelism there with shared memory and no pickling.
  • Cost: preemptive switching means data races on shared state (x += 1 is not atomic); unbounded pools exhaust memory and file descriptors.
  • From async code: await asyncio.to_thread(sync_fn, arg) (3.9+) runs it on the loop's default executor.

stages.name: Where processes win
stages.html:
"Processes are the only way to run Python bytecode on several cores in standard CPython."

You get You pay
One interpreter and one GIL per process → true parallelism arguments and results are pickled across the boundary
Isolation: a crash or leak stays in one worker start-up time per process
memory per process: a model loaded in 8 workers is 8 copies 
worth it when:   work per task  ≫  cost of pickling its inputs and outputs
  • Each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL, so Python bytecode runs on several cores.
  • Cost: arguments and results are pickled across the boundary; each process pays startup and holds its own copy of anything it loads (a model loaded in 8 workers is 8 copies).
  • spawn vs fork changes startup and memory (see multiprocessing-linux-vs-mac).
  • Rule of thumb: worth it when each task does far more work than it costs to pickle its inputs.

stages.name: What I'd pick for an AI backend
stages.claim: all three, each in its lane
stages.html:
"Async at the edge, threads for sync stragglers, processes or a worker tier for Python CPU work."

  • Version note: 3.13's free-threaded build (python3.13t) makes threads viable for Python CPU work, but only once every C extension you use supports it.

followUps.question: 🧪 What does this print, and roughly how long does it take?  then
followUps.html:
Nothing is printed, and it takes about 3 seconds, not 1.

f() #1: time.sleep(1) blocks the thread ── the loop can't switch ──▶ returns after 1 s
f() #2: starts only now ───────────────────────────────────────────▶ 2 s
f() #3: ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ 3 s
with await asyncio.sleep(1): all three wait together → about 1 s

followUps.question: "Threads are useless in Python because of the GIL, right?"
followUps.html:
No. Threads overlap blocking I/O and run in parallel inside C extensions.

Work Threads help?
Blocking I/O the GIL is released while waiting
C extensions that release the GIL
Python bytecode on two cores

followUps.question: Why not just use asyncio for everything?
followUps.html:
It only helps waiting, and only if every call on the path is async.

Situation asyncio alone
A CPU loop inside a coroutine blocks the loop, exactly like time.sleep
A sync-only SDK needs a thread anyway
Python-heavy CPU work needs processes

followUps.question: How big should the thread pool be for sync calls to an LLM provider?
followUps.html:
Size it by concurrency, not by cores.

in flight ≈ throughput × latency           ← Little's law
10 req/s × 2 s = 20 threads
cap by: the provider's rate limit, and memory
default to_thread executor = min(32, cpu_count + 4) threads   ← set your own when it matters

followUps.question: Your FastAPI service does async calls plus a 300 ms pure-Python post-processing step. Design it.
followUps.html:
Keep the provider calls async; move the 300 ms step off the loop.

Post-processing inputs Where it runs
Small to pickle, steady load a ProcessPoolExecutor via loop.run_in_executor
Spiky, or needs its own scaling a queue to a worker service

Watch event-loop lag and p99 before and after: the win shows up as tail latency.

followUps.question: Does 3.13 free-threading change your answer?
followUps.html:
For I/O, no. For Python CPU work, possibly, once the ecosystem is ready.

Workload With python3.13t
I/O-bound asyncio is still the right tool
Python CPU work threads could replace processes and avoid pickling
Condition every C extension ships free-threaded wheels; the single-thread slowdown is measured

Today: a pilot on a batch job, not the API.

dontSay: "asyncio is always faster." — it's only better at waiting.
"Threads don't work in Python." — they do for I/O and C-heavy work.
"Use multiprocessing for I/O." — it pays process and pickling costs for nothing.
Choosing before measuring where the time goes.

python-q3.testing: whether you can name definition-time evaluation, not just the symptom.
python-q3.trap: "Python keeps the list between calls" with no explanation of why.
python-q3.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "A function like def add, item, bucket equals empty list, returns a list with one, then one-two, then one-two-three. The list grows between calls."
2 · Trace it step by step "That's because the def statement evaluates the default once and stores the resulting object on the function, in dunder-defaults. Every call that doesn't pass the argument binds its local name to that same object, and append mutates it in place."
3 · The rule that decides it "The rule is that default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, not each time it's called. Immutable defaults are safe; mutable ones are shared."
4 · Variants that flip the answer "The fix is a sentinel: default to None and build the list inside the body. If None is a valid input, I use a private object as the sentinel. The same root cause shows up as a class attribute list, or a timestamp default frozen at import."
5 · The production version "In a service it's worse than a quirk. The default lives as long as the worker process, so it becomes accidental global state shared across requests and even tenants. A lint rule catches it."
Close "Defaults are evaluated at def time; use None and build inside."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
Call Passes bucket? Returns
add(1) no → the shared default [1]
add(2) no → the same list [1, 2]
add(3, []) yes → its own list [3]
add(4) no → back to the shared one [1, 2, 4] 
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
print(add(1)); print(add(2)); print(add(3, [])); print(add(4))
# → [1]
# → [1, 2]
# → [3]
# → [1, 2, 4]

"The third call passes its own list, so it's clean. The fourth goes back to the shared default."

stages.name: Trace it step by step
stages.claim: one object, stored on the function
stages.html:
"One list object, created once, reached from two places."

Step What runs add.__defaults__
def executes [] is evaluated once and stored on the function ([],)
add(1) local bucket → that object; .append(1) mutates it ([1],)
add(2) the same object again ([1, 2],)
Mutate or rebind:bucket.append(x) changes the shared objectleaks · bucket = bucket + [x] makes a new listdoesn't
  • def runs → evaluates [] → stores it in add.__defaults__.
  • Each call without bucket binds the local name to that same object.
  • .append mutates it in place; rebinding (bucket = bucket + [x]) would not.

Prove it:

def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item); return bucket
print(add.__defaults__)
add(1); add(2)
print(add.__defaults__)
print(add(9) is add.__defaults__[0])
# → ([],)
# → ([1, 2],)
# → True

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html:
"Default expressions run at definition time."

Default Safe? Why
0, None, "x", a tuple can't be mutated
[], {}, set() one shared, mutable object
datetime.now(), uuid4() one value, frozen when the module is imported
  • Language guarantee: default expressions are evaluated once, left to right, when the function is defined.
  • Immutable defaults (0, None, "x", tuples) are safe because they can't be mutated.
  • Fix:
_MISSING = object()
def add(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

stages.name: Variants that flip the answer
stages.html:
Variant Shared? Why
def f(ts=datetime.now()) yes, frozen timestamp evaluated once at import
class A: items = [] yes, across instances class attribute, mutated via self.items.append
@dataclass with items: list = [] error dataclasses reject it; use field(default_factory=list)
Pydantic field tags: list = [] no Pydantic copies defaults per instance
def f(x=None) then x = x or [] subtle bug an empty list passed in is replaced too

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
"In a worker, 'between calls' means 'between requests'."

Pattern What leaks
def call(url, headers={}) and a helper adds an auth header one tenant's token is sent on another tenant's request
def handle(event, seen=[]) grows for the life of the process: a slow memory leak
def log(msg, ts=time.time()) every log line carries the start-up time
Guard:ruff B006 (mutable default)B008 (function call in a default)both in CI
  • In a long-running FastAPI or Celery worker, a mutable default lives for the process lifetime: one request's data appears in another's.
  • A default headers={} that a helper mutates can leak an auth header between tenants.
  • Guard: ruff rule B006 (flake8-bugbear) flags mutable defaults; B008 flags function calls in defaults.

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints?  then
followUps.html:
1 2 2.

f(2): cache = {2: 4}          → len 1
f(3): cache = {2: 4, 3: 9}    → len 2      ← the same dict as before
f(2): overwrites key 2        → len 2

This is the "intentional" use: a mutable default as a memo cache. functools.lru_cache is explicit and bounded.

followUps.question: Why did Python choose def-time evaluation?
followUps.html:
It's simple and fast: defaults are computed once.

Design Cost
Def-time (Python) one evaluation; one rule for every expression
Call-time re-run arbitrary code on each call; capture its scope

PEP 671 proposed late-bound defaults (=>) and wasn't accepted.

followUps.question: "So mutable defaults are always wrong?"
followUps.html:
Almost always, in application code.

Case Verdict
A default that gets mutated a bug
A memo dict in a tiny script; a default never mutated deliberate, and still unclear to the next reader
None sentinel or an explicit cache the clear form

followUps.question: What's wrong with ?
followUps.html:
An empty list passed by the caller is falsy, so it gets replaced.

mine = []
add(1, mine)          # inside: bucket = bucket or []  → a NEW list
mine                  # still []          ← the caller's list was never filled

Test for "not passed" with if bucket is None.

followUps.question: Where have you seen this cause a real incident pattern?
followUps.html:
The pattern is state leaking across requests in a long-lived worker.

Shape:a default dict of headers or contextmutated per requestone user's data in another's responseonly under load
Fix:the sentinela lint rule in CI so it can't return

dontSay: "Python caches the list between calls." — it's one object created at def time.
"Defaults are evaluated each call." — they're not.
"Use x = x or []." — it breaks on empty inputs.

python-q4.testing: identity vs equality, and whether you know interning is a CPython detail.
python-q4.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Double-equals asks whether two objects have equal values, by calling dunder-eq. Is asks whether they are the same object, which can't be overridden."
2 · What CPython does "Is sometimes looks right by accident, because CPython caches some objects. Small integers from minus five to two fifty-six are preallocated, and short identifier-like strings are often interned. That's an implementation detail, not a language rule."
3 · Prove it "So two variables holding one hundred are the same object, and two holding a thousand built at runtime are not, though they're equal."
4 · Where it bites in production "I use is only for singletons and sentinels: None, enum members, and my own missing-object sentinel. For everything else, double-equals. A status code compared with is can pass in tests and fail in production."
5 · What changes by version "Since 3.8 CPython warns when is is used with a literal, and linters flag it."
Close "Equality for values, identity for singletons."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"== compares values through __eq__; is compares identity and can't be overloaded."

== is
Asks are the values equal? are these the same object?
How type(a).__eq__(a, b), then the reflected call, then identity compares identity: id(a) == id(b) while both are alive
Can a class change it? yes, by defining __eq__ no
Use for values singletons and sentinels
  • a == b → type(a).__eq__(a, b), falls back to b.__eq__(a), then identity.
  • a is b → same object; id(a) == id(b) while both are alive.

stages.name: What CPython does
stages.claim: caches that make is pass by luck
stages.html:
"Three caches make is pass by luck."

Cache (all CPython details) What it shares
Small-int cache −5 … 256 are preallocated singletons
String interning identifier-like literals and names, at compile time; sys.intern() on request
Constant folding equal literals in one code object may share one constant
Point What it means
Small int cache (CPython detail) −5..256 are preallocated singletons.
String interning (CPython detail) identifier-like literals and names are interned at compile time; sys.intern() does it explicitly.
Constant folding equal literals in the same code object may share one constant.
Expression Result Guaranteed?
x is None reliable yes, None is a singleton
256 is 256-style small ints usually True no, CPython detail
int("1000") is int("1000") False no
[] is [] False yes, two new lists

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Name Built by Value Same object as its twin?
a, b int("256") at runtime 256 hits the small-int cache
c, d int("257") at runtime 257 two objects, equal values
s, t "".join(…) against a literal "abc" until sys.intern(s) 
a = int("256"); b = int("256")
c = int("257"); d = int("257")
print(a is b, c is d, c == d)
s = "".join(["ab", "c"]); t = "abc"
print(s == t, s is t, __import__("sys").intern(s) is t)
# → True False True
# → True False True

int("…") builds the value at runtime, so constant folding can't help: 256 hits the cache, 257 doesn't.

stages.name: Where it bites in production
stages.html:
"Legitimate uses are few; the bugs are common."

Code Verdict Why
if x is None None is a guaranteed singleton
status is Status.DONE, x is _MISSING enum members and sentinels are single objects
type(x) is dict an exact type check
response.status_code is 200 passes only while the int is cached; SyntaxWarning since 3.8
if arr == 0: (NumPy) == returns an array: "truth value is ambiguous"
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 floats need math.isclose
Point What it means
Legit if x is None, sentinel objects, enum members (status is Status.DONE), type(x) is dict for exact type checks.
Bug if response.status_code is 200 passes in tests with small values cached and is a SyntaxWarning since 3.8; compare with ==.
Bug NumPy/pandas: arr == 0 returns an array, so if arr == 0 raises "truth value is ambiguous"; is there is wrong too. Use .all()/.any() or np.array_equal.
Floats == on floats needs tolerance: math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3).
NaN float("nan") == float("nan") is False, but x is x is True, which is why [nan] == [nan] is True (containers check identity first).

stages.name: What changes by version
stages.claim: a warning in 3.8, immortal objects in 3.12
stages.html:

python-q7.testing: whether you understand cooperative scheduling well enough to predict when concurrency happens and when it doesn't.
python-q7.trap: "async runs things in the background" or "on another thread."

    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print(name, "end")

    await asyncio.gather(worker("B", 0.2), worker("C", 0.1))

Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "In CPython the main mechanism is reference counting, with a cyclic garbage collector as a backstop for reference cycles."
2 · What CPython does "Every object has a count of references to it. When a name is rebound or a container drops it, the count goes down, and at zero the object is freed immediately. Counting can't free cycles, so a collector tracks container objects in generations and periodically frees groups that are only reachable from each other."

4 · Where it bites in production "Two things people get wrong. Freeing an object doesn't return memory to the OS: small objects live in arenas that are released only when completely empty, so RSS often stays high. And the collector is tunable: gc-freeze before forking workers avoids copy-on-write."

def timed(fn):
    if inspect.iscoroutinefunction(fn):
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        async def aw(*a, **k):
            t = time.perf_counter()
            try: return await fn(*a, **k)
            finally: print(fn.__name__, f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")
        return aw
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def w(*a, **k):
        t = time.perf_counter()
        try: return fn(*a, **k)
        finally: print(fn.__name__, f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")
    return w
@timed
async def fetch(): await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
asyncio.run(fetch())
# → fetch 0.20s

Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Semantically a with block is a try-finally: enter acquires, exit is guaranteed to run. The difference is where the cleanup logic lives."

from contextlib import contextmanager
@contextmanager
def transaction(log):
    log.append("begin")
    try:

    except Exception:

spine: What I'd pick for an AI backend
python-q14.testing: structured concurrency, and whether you know that gather leaves siblings running on failure.
python-q14.trap: a bare except Exception or except BaseException that swallows CancelledError.
python-q14.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Both run several awaitables concurrently as Tasks. The difference is what happens when one fails."
2 · Where gather still fits "With gather, the first exception propagates to the caller, but the other tasks are not cancelled. They keep running in the background and their results are lost. With return-exceptions true, nothing propagates and I get a list mixing results and exceptions. That still fits best-effort fan-out."
3 · Where TaskGroup wins "TaskGroup, from 3.11, is structured concurrency. The block doesn't exit until every task finishes. If one fails, the group cancels the rest, waits for them, and raises an ExceptionGroup with every real failure. No orphans."
4 · How cancellation actually works "Cancellation is cooperative: cancel throws CancelledError into the coroutine at its current await. Cleanup goes in finally, and the error must propagate. A bare except swallows it, and then timeouts stop working."
5 · What I'd pick for an AI backend "For fan-out in a service I default to TaskGroup with asyncio-timeout, and wrap each task when the work is best-effort."
Close "Gather leaves orphans on failure; TaskGroup owns its tasks."

Pre-3.11 code; libraries supporting older Pythons gather, with explicit cancellation of the rest on failure

  • Pre-3.11 codebases. Libraries that must support older Pythons.

stages.name: Where TaskGroup wins
stages.html:
Time Task a (fails at 0.1 s) Task b (needs 0.5 s) With TaskGroup With gather
0.1 s raises ValueError sleeping the group cancels b the error goes to the caller
0.1 s+ — CancelledError → cleanup → re-raise waits for b to wind down b keeps running, unobserved
exit raises ExceptionGroup([ValueError('a')]) —

Prove it:

import asyncio
async def job(name, delay, fail=False):
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(delay)
        if fail: raise ValueError(name)
        print(name, "done")
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print(name, "cancelled"); raise
async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(job("a", 0.1, fail=True)); tg.create_task(job("b", 0.5))
    except* ValueError as eg:
        print("failed:", [str(e) for e in eg.exceptions])
asyncio.run(main())
# → b cancelled
# → failed: ['a']

With gather instead, ValueError reaches main after 0.1 s while b keeps running unobserved.

stages.name: How cancellation actually works
stages.html:
Cancel:task.cancel()at the task's next resumptionCancelledError raised at the await where it's parkedfinally / async with clean upre-raise
Code in the coroutine Catches CancelledError? Result
except Exception: no (it's a BaseException since 3.8) cancellation works
except asyncio.CancelledError: …; raise yes, then re-raises cancellation works, with cleanup
except BaseException: pass or bare except: pass yes, and swallows it the task keeps running; timeout() never fires; shutdown hangs
  • task.cancel() → at the task's next resumption, CancelledError is raised at the await where it's parked.
  • Cleanup belongs in finally / async with. Re-raise after logging.
  • asyncio.timeout() and TaskGroup rely on cancellation propagating; they convert it to TimeoutError or the group's error.
  • Swallowing it: except BaseException: pass, or except: pass → the task keeps running, timeout() never fires its error, shutdown hangs.
  • asyncio.shield(aw) protects an inner operation from the outer cancel (e.g. finish writing an audit record).

python-q15.testing: schema-first structured output, validation on receipt, and bounded repair.
python-q15.trap: regex-parsing prose, or an unbounded "ask again until it works" loop.
python-q15.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Constraints "I don't parse prose. The output drives code, so a wrong shape is a crash and a right shape with a wrong meaning is a bad action. Both have to be caught before execution."
2 · Runtime model "I define the shape first as a Pydantic model and use it at both ends. On the way out it generates a JSON Schema that I pass as a tool definition or a structured-output schema, and most providers constrain decoding to it. On the way in I still validate."
3 · The hard part "Because schema-valid isn't semantically valid. The JSON can match the shape and still name an order that doesn't exist. Those are validators on the model. When validation fails I do a bounded repair: the structured error goes back to the model once or twice, with the field path."
4 · Failure modes "After that I fail loudly with a typed error and route to a fallback. Never an infinite loop. And the executor accepts only the validated object, against an allow-list of actions."
5 · What I'd monitor "I'd monitor the validation-failure rate per model and prompt version, and repair rounds per request."
Close "Schema out, validation in, bounded repair, allow-listed execution."

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html:
Output is If it's wrong Caught by
The wrong shape a crash in the parser or executor schema-constrained decoding + validation
The right shape, wrong meaning a bad action is executed validators and business checks
A dangerous action data loss, a refund to the wrong person an allow-list and permission check in the executor

Budget: each repair round costs one more model call.

  • Output is parsed by code and then executed: a tool call, a DB filter, a workflow step.
  • Wrong shape = crash; right shape, wrong meaning = a bad action. Both must be caught before execution.
  • Budget: each repair round costs a model call.

stages.html:

stages.name: The hard part
stages.html:
Check {"action":"refund","order_id":"ord_9","amount":20}
Valid JSON
Matches the schema (action, order_id: str, amount: float)
order_id is a known order ('order_id',) — "unknown order"
Repair:e.errors() (field path + message)back to the modelvalidate againat most max_repairs = 2then a typed LLMOutputError, with the raw output logged

Prove it — shape passes, meaning fails:

from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator, ValidationError
ALLOWED_IDS = {"ord_1", "ord_2"}
class Refund(BaseModel):
    action: Literal["refund"]
    order_id: str
    amount: float
    @field_validator("order_id")
    @classmethod
    def known(cls, v):
        if v not in ALLOWED_IDS: raise ValueError("unknown order")
        return v
try: Refund.model_validate_json('{"action":"refund","order_id":"ord_9","amount":20}')
except ValidationError as e: print(e.errors()[0]["loc"], e.errors()[0]["msg"])
# → ('order_id',) Value error, unknown order
  • Repair prompt carries e.errors() (field path + message), not the whole traceback.
  • Cap it: max_repairs = 2. Then raise LLMOutputError with the last raw output logged for debugging.

python-q16.testing: that one blocking call stalls every request on the loop, and that you can find and fix it.
python-q16.trap: blaming worker count or the database, instead of naming the stalled event loop.
python-q16.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the symptom "It blocks the whole event loop, not just that request. The symptom is distinctive: p99 collapses under load and throughput caps, while CPU looks mostly idle and the downstream looks fine. Health checks can time out too."
2 · Measure before guessing "The reason is that an async worker runs every in-flight request on one thread. So I measure event-loop lag: how late a scheduled callback actually runs."
3 · Rank the suspects "The suspects are a sync HTTP client like requests, a sync database driver, time-sleep, reading a big file, or a CPU-heavy loop."
4 · Confirm "To confirm, asyncio debug mode logs any callback that holds the loop longer than a hundred milliseconds, and py-spy dump on a live worker shows the exact frame the loop thread is stuck in."
5 · Fix "The fix is an async client; or for a sync-only library, asyncio to-thread; or a process pool for CPU work. In FastAPI a plain def handler runs in a threadpool automatically."
6 · Guard against the next one "Then I guard it with a lint rule for blocking calls in async code and an alert on loop lag."
Close "One blocking call stalls every request on that worker; find it with loop lag and py-spy."

stages.name: Read the symptom
stages.html:
Observation Reading
p50 and p99 climb together under concurrency; RPS plateaus requests are queuing behind something
Worker CPU is low the blocker is waiting on I/O, synchronously
One core pegged at 100% the blocker is CPU work
Downstream metrics are healthy the wait is inside this process
Health probes time out now and then the loop can't even answer /health 
throughput cap ≈ 1 request per blocking duration, per worker
a 500 ms blocking call → about 2 requests/s per worker, whatever the concurrency
  • p99 and p50 climb together under concurrency; RPS plateaus.
  • Worker CPU low (it's waiting on I/O, synchronously) — or pegged at 100% of one core if the blocker is CPU work.
  • Downstream metrics healthy. Health/readiness probes time out intermittently.

stages.name: Measure before guessing
stages.html:
Tick Should fire after Actually late by Why
1 0.1 s 0.4 s bad_handler held the loop for 0.5 s
2 0.1 s 0.0 s the loop is free again
3 0.1 s 0.0 s

Prove it — a heartbeat that should tick every 100 ms:

import asyncio, time
async def heartbeat():
    for _ in range(3):
        t = time.perf_counter(); await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        print(f"tick late by {time.perf_counter() - t - 0.1:.1f}s")
async def bad_handler():
    time.sleep(0.5)                       # blocking: holds the loop
async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(heartbeat(), bad_handler())
asyncio.run(main())
# → tick late by 0.4s
# → tick late by 0.0s
# → tick late by 0.0s

One blocking call delayed an unrelated coroutine by 0.4 s. Export that lag as a metric in production.

A sync-only library a thread await asyncio.to_thread(fn, …), or a plain def handler

@app.get("/a")                                   # sync lib → thread
async def a(): return await asyncio.to_thread(vendor_sdk.call, "x")

def c(): return vendor_sdk.call("x")

  • CPU-bound → ProcessPoolExecutor or a worker tier (see cpu-preprocessing-next-to-async-api).

More workers

A request on a blocked worker still stalls

Handler Runs on May block?

A sync library inside async def the event loop the worst of both

Horizon Action

Long term call the vendor's HTTP API with httpx.AsyncClient, or isolate the SDK behind its own small service
Metric the executor's queue length

Hidden blocker Where
A logging handler that sends over HTTP every log call
A sync token refresh inside an auth library
DNS resolution some clients

python-q17.testing: a decision ladder by hold time and GIL behaviour, and the costs of each rung.
python-q17.trap: a process pool for everything, even work that pickles badly or holds huge models.
python-q17.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Constraints "Never inline in the handler. CPU work inside an async def holds the loop and delays every other request. The constraint is to keep loop lag to a few milliseconds."
2 · Runtime model "Where it goes is a ladder, decided by how long it holds the CPU and whether that time is in Python bytecode or in C. C code that releases the GIL, like NumPy or a Rust tokenizer: a thread through to-thread is enough. Pure Python for tens to hundreds of milliseconds: a process pool. Seconds, spiky, or GPU: a queue and a separate worker fleet."
3 · The hard part "The hard part is the process boundary. Arguments and results are pickled, so I pass a path or a key, not a fifty-megabyte document. And every process holds its own copy of whatever it loads."
4 · Failure modes "Each wrong placement has its own symptom: a CPU loop in the handler shows as loop lag; a thread pool for pure Python gives no speed-up; a pool per request costs seconds."
5 · What I'd monitor "I'd monitor loop lag, the executor's queue depth, and the worker queue's depth and oldest job."
Close "Measure the hold time, then pick the rung: thread for C, process for Python, queue for long or spiky."

Input and output size the pickling cost across a process boundary
Memory footprint multiplied by the number of processes
  • The async API must keep loop lag under a few ms to hold its p99.
  • The preprocessing step: its duration, where its CPU time goes (Python vs C), input/output size, and memory footprint.

stages.html:
Hold time / kind Where Cost
< ~1 ms inline none worth paying
C code, GIL released asyncio.to_thread / thread pool thread count; shared memory is a plus
Python bytecode, 10 ms–1 s ProcessPoolExecutor pickling; memory per process; startup
seconds, spiky, GPU queue → worker service infra, at-least-once semantics, job status API

Prove it — pure-Python CPU work in a process pool keeps the loop free:

import asyncio, time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
def parse(n): return sum(i * i for i in range(n))       # pure Python
async def heartbeat():
    t = time.perf_counter(); await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    print(f"loop lag {time.perf_counter() - t - 0.05:.2f}s")
async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(2) as pool:
        await asyncio.gather(loop.run_in_executor(pool, parse, 5_000_000), heartbeat())
if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main())
# → loop lag 0.00s   (call parse() inline instead and the lag equals its runtime)

spine: What I'd pick for an AI backend
python-q18.testing: that you treat __slots__ as a measured memory optimisation, not a style rule.
python-q18.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Slots tell CPython to store an instance's attributes in fixed slots in the object itself, in place of a per-instance dict. It trades flexibility for memory."
2 · Where __slots__ wins "The win is memory: no dict per instance, which matters with millions of small objects, like records in a batch. Attribute access also gets slightly faster."
3 · Where it costs you "The costs: I can't add attributes that aren't declared, so some libraries break. Weak references need their own slot. Multiple inheritance gets awkward. And a subclass without its own slots gets a dict back, silently undoing the saving."
4 · The deciding question "So it's a profiling-led decision. With a dozen service objects it's pointless. With ten million records I'd first ask whether they should be objects at all."
5 · What I'd pick for an AI backend "A NumPy array or a DataFrame with one column per field usually beats any per-object layout. If they must be objects, dataclass with slots true is the clean way."
Close "Measure first; columnar before slots; slots for the last stretch."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"Slots trade the per-instance dict for fixed storage: less memory, fewer freedoms."

normal instance:   [ header | → __dict__ ] ──▶ { "x": 1, "y": 2 }      a dict per instance
slotted instance:  [ header | x | y ]                                   fixed offsets, no dict
Normal class __slots__
Per-instance dict yes no
New attributes at runtime yes no
Memory per instance more less

stages.name: Where `__slots__` wins
stages.html:
Class Bytes per object (100,000 instances, tracemalloc)
P (normal) 119
S (__slots__) 87

Measured on CPython 3.12, M-series Mac; the figure includes the int values and the list slot.

Prove it — measured with tracemalloc:

import tracemalloc
class P:
    def __init__(s, x, y): s.x, s.y = x, y
class S:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")
    def __init__(s, x, y): s.x, s.y = x, y
for cls in (P, S):

2 · The layers "There are three layers. 4 · Failure modes "The failures are the cache being down, a stampede when a hot key expires, and an unbounded in-process cache."

import os
from functools import lru_cache
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def lookup(k): return k * 2
def worker(k):
    lookup(k); return os.getpid(), lookup.cache_info().currsize
if __name__ == "__main__":
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(4) as ex:
        last = dict(ex.map(worker, range(400), chunksize=1))

python-q24.testing: an atomic claim of the key, a state machine for concurrent duplicates, and response replay.
python-q24.trap: storing the key after the side effect.
python-q24.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Constraints "Clients retry on timeouts, and the network can drop a response after the server committed. So the client sends an Idempotency-Key header, generated once per logical operation, and the server must execute once per key."
2 · Runtime model "The flow is claim, execute, record. I atomically claim the key by inserting a row with status in-progress under a unique constraint. If the insert succeeds I run the operation and store the response against the key. If it conflicts and the row is complete, I replay the stored response; if it's still in progress I return a 409."
3 · The hard part "The subtle part is the crash window. I write the key's final state in the same transaction as the side effect, so a crash can't leave one without the other. For an external effect like a payment, I pass the key through to the provider, or record intermediate state and reconcile."
4 · Failure modes "Other mistakes: a key scoped globally instead of per tenant, replaying a stored 500, and the same key with a different body, which I answer with 422."
5 · What I'd monitor "I'd monitor the replay rate, stuck in-progress claims and body mismatches."
Close "Claim atomically, record with the effect, replay on retry."

stages.html:

Clients retry on timeouts the same request arrives twice
A response can be lost after the commit the client can't know whether it happened
The operation has a side effect (create an order, charge, start an expensive job) it must happen once

  • The operation has a side effect that must happen once: create an order, charge, send, start an expensive job.

stages.html:

import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE idem (tenant TEXT, key TEXT, status TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (tenant, key))")
CLAIM = "INSERT INTO idem VALUES (?, ?, 'in_progress') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING key"
print(db.execute(CLAIM, ("t1", "k1")).fetchall())    # first request
print(db.execute(CLAIM, ("t1", "k1")).fetchall())    # retry / concurrent duplicate
print(db.execute(CLAIM, ("t2", "k1")).fetchall())    # same key, other tenant
# → [('k1',)]
# → []
# → [('k1',)]

The primary key on (tenant, key) makes the database the arbiter; two concurrent requests can't both get a row back.

external effect (payment, LLM job) pass the key to the provider, or record "started" and reconcile

python-q25.testing: burst behaviour of each algorithm, and a correct distributed implementation.
python-q25.trap: a per-process limiter that silently multiplies the limit by the number of workers.
python-q25.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "The choice comes down to how much burst I allow and how much state I can afford per key."
2 · The four algorithms "A fixed window counts requests per clock minute. It's trivial, but at the boundary a client can send the full limit twice within a second. A sliding window smooths that at the cost of more state. A token bucket refills at a steady rate up to a capacity, so a client can burst and is then held to the refill rate. That's usually right for APIs. A leaky bucket smooths output to a fixed rate."
3 · Making it distributed "In production it must be distributed. With eight workers and four pods, an in-process limiter allows thirty-two times the limit. So the state goes in Redis, updated atomically with a Lua script, and I decide up front whether to fail open or closed when Redis is down."
4 · The deciding question "The deciding question is what I'm protecting: my own capacity from clients, a fragile upstream from me, or fair shares between tenants."
5 · What I'd pick for an AI backend "For LLM APIs I limit on two things per tenant: requests per minute and tokens per minute, because one huge prompt costs more than a hundred small ones."
Close "Token bucket per tenant, in Redis, on requests and on tokens."

stages.html:
Call Tokens before Allowed? Tokens after
1–5 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 the burst 4, 3, 2, 1, 0
6, 7 ≈ 0 ≈ 0

8 1 0

allow  if tokens ≥ cost, then tokens −= cost           ← cost = 1 per request, or the LLM token count

Prove it — a burst of 5, then held to the refill rate:

import time
class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate, capacity):
        self.rate, self.cap, self.tokens, self.t = rate, capacity, capacity, time.monotonic()
    def allow(self, cost=1):
        now = time.monotonic()
        self.tokens = min(self.cap, self.tokens + (now - self.t) * self.rate); self.t = now
        if self.tokens >= cost: self.tokens -= cost; return True
        return False
b = TokenBucket(rate=2, capacity=5)
print([b.allow() for _ in range(7)]); time.sleep(0.5); print(b.allow())
# → [True, True, True, True, True, False, False]
# → True

cost lets the same bucket charge by tokens for LLM requests.

python-q26.testing: ExceptionGroup/except*, and an explicit policy for partial success.
python-q26.trap: gather with default settings, surfacing only the first error and losing the rest.
python-q26.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Constraints "First I decide the policy, because the code follows from it. Is this all-or-nothing, where any failure makes the answer wrong? Or best-effort, where three of five sources are good enough and I report the other two?"
2 · Runtime model "For all-or-nothing I use a TaskGroup. If any task fails it cancels the rest and raises an ExceptionGroup containing every failure. I handle it with except-star, which matches by type inside the group: a timeout marks a provider as slow, an auth error pages someone."
3 · The hard part "For best-effort I don't want one failure to cancel the others, so each task catches its own exception and returns a result object. Then I apply the policy: if a quorum succeeded, I respond with the partial result and the list of failed sources."
4 · Failure modes "The mistakes are gather's default, which gives the first error only, and return-exceptions with nobody checking the list."
5 · What I'd monitor "I log each failure with the provider name as a structured field, and count failures per provider, which feeds the circuit breaker."
Close "Policy first; TaskGroup for all-or-nothing, per-task results for best-effort; never one collapsed error."

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html:
Policy When On one failure
All-or-nothing each result feeds the final answer; a missing piece changes its meaning cancel the rest; fail the request
Best-effort multi-source retrieval, price comparison, redundant providers keep the rest; report what's missing

Both run under one time budget for the whole fan-out, not per call.

  • All-or-nothing: tool steps that each feed the final answer; a missing piece changes meaning.
  • Best-effort: multi-source retrieval, price comparisons, redundant providers.
  • A time budget for the whole fan-out, not per call.

stages.name: Runtime model
stages.html:
Task Outcome Handled by
a, c, e return (or are cancelled once a sibling fails) —
b TimeoutError except* TimeoutError → "slow"
d PermissionError except* PermissionError → "auth"

Every matching except* clause runs, each with its sub-group.

Prove it — all failures surfaced, handled by type:

import asyncio
async def call(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    if name == "b": raise TimeoutError(name)
    if name == "d": raise PermissionError(name)
    return name
async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            for n in "abcde": tg.create_task(call(n))
    except* TimeoutError as g: print("slow:", [str(e) for e in g.exceptions])
    except* PermissionError as g: print("auth:", [str(e) for e in g.exceptions])
asyncio.run(main())
# → slow: ['b']
# → auth: ['d']

Both failures reach the handler. With gather, only the first raised exception would.

stages.name: The hard part
stages.html:
Best-effort:each task wraps its own callreturns {src, ok, data or error}collectok count ≥ quorum?partial result + "degraded": [...]DegradedError
async def safe(name):
    try: return {"src": name, "ok": True, "data": await call(name)}
    except Exception as e: return {"src": name, "ok": False, "error": type(e).__name__}
async with asyncio.timeout(3):
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(safe(n)) for n in providers]
results = [t.result() for t in tasks]
ok = [r for r in results if r["ok"]]
if len(ok) < QUORUM: raise DegradedError(results)
  • Response carries "degraded": ["b", "d"] so the UI or the LLM prompt can say what's missing.
  • safe catches Exception, not BaseException, so cancellation still propagates.

Mistake Effect
gather default first error only; other tasks keep running
gather(return_exceptions=True) unchecked failures silently treated as results

per-call timeouts only total latency = slowest call; set an overall budget
no per-provider breaker a dead provider costs its timeout on every request

stages.html:

unmatched exceptions are re-raised in a new group

python-q27.testing: nominal vs structural typing, and the limits of runtime_checkable.
python-q27.trap: treating isinstance against a runtime_checkable Protocol as real validation.
python-q27.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "An ABC is nominal typing: a class is a Retriever because it inherits from Retriever. A Protocol is structural typing: any class with the right methods counts, without inheriting anything."
2 · Where Protocol wins "Protocol wins when I don't own the types or don't want to couple them: third-party clients, test fakes, adapters for different vector stores or LLM providers. My code depends on the shape it needs, and the check happens in the type checker."
3 · Where ABC wins "ABC wins when I own the hierarchy and want runtime enforcement or shared behaviour. It refuses to instantiate until the abstract methods exist, and it can carry a template method implemented once."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: do I own the implementers, and do they share code?"
5 · What I'd pick for an AI backend "For an AI backend: Protocols for the ports, like Embedder and VectorStore, and ABCs for internal plugin hierarchies with a shared lifecycle."
Close "One trap: runtime-checkable only checks that the method names exist, not their signatures."

python-q28.testing: separating a leak from fragmentation from legitimate growth, with the right tool for each.
python-q28.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the symptom "First I separate three things that all look like rising RSS: a true leak, where objects stay referenced; fragmentation, where memory is freed but not returned to the OS; and legitimate growth, like a cache filling up. I plot RSS against request count, not only time."
2 · Measure before guessing "Then I compare Python-level memory with RSS. With tracemalloc I take a snapshot after warm-up, run load, take another, and diff them by line. If traced memory grows with RSS, it's Python objects. If it's flat while RSS grows, it's fragmentation or native memory, and I switch to memray."
3 · Rank the suspects "The usual suspects: an unbounded module-level dict, an lru-cache on a method that pins self, closures capturing large objects, and tasks that never finish."
4 · Confirm "To confirm who holds the objects, I use objgraph back-references or gc get-referrers on a sample of the growing type."
5 · Fix "The fix is usually a bound: a maxsize, a TTL, or weak references."
6 · Guard against the next one "And the guard is a memory-per-request metric plus a soak test."
Close "Leak, fragmentation or growth; let the tracemalloc diff name the line."

stages.name: Read the symptom
stages.html:
RSS shape Likely
Grows with request count, never plateaus leak / unbounded structure
Jumps on big requests, stays high, then flat fragmentation / allocator retention
Grows then plateaus at a bound a cache filling up (legit)
Grows with time, not traffic background task or timer accumulating

stages.name: Measure before guessing
stages.html:
Prove it — the diff names the line that's growing:

import tracemalloc
CACHE = {}
def handle(i): CACHE[i] = bytes(1000)           # the "leak": unbounded module-level dict
tracemalloc.start()
for i in range(1000): handle(i)
before = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for i in range(1000, 11000): handle(i)
after = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
top = after.compare_to(before, "lineno")[0]
print(top.traceback[0].lineno, f"+{top.size_diff / 1e6:.0f} MB")
# → 3 +11 MB   (CPython 3.12)

Line 3 grew by ~11 MB between snapshots: 10,000 new 1 KB objects plus the dict's growth. (A constant like "x" * 1000 would be folded into one shared object and hide the leak.) In a service, expose snapshot-and-diff behind an admin endpoint, or run it in a staging soak test.

stages.name: Rank the suspects
stages.html:
Rank Suspect Signature
1 An unbounded module-level dict or list (cache, registry, "seen" set) grows with distinct keys
2 @cache / @lru_cache(maxsize=None), or either on a method pins every self
3 Closures or callbacks on a long-lived object, never removed grows with registrations
4 Tasks never awaited; exceptions stored with tracebacks frames kept alive
5 Native memory: a C extension, large arrays held by a cache traced memory flat, RSS grows
6 Fragmentation after a very large request a step up, then flat

python-q29.testing: that you size from the workload shape and memory, then verify with a load test.
python-q29.trap: "2 × cores + 1" recited for an async service, or scaling workers when one call is blocking the loop.
python-q29.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Constraints "It depends on the workload shape, so I start there: the cores and memory the container actually has, whether the work is async I/O, sync I/O or CPU, and the model size."
2 · Runtime model "For an async ASGI service, each worker runs one event loop, and one loop holds hundreds of concurrent I/O-bound requests. So workers are about using cores, not about concurrency: roughly one per core. For a sync framework, concurrency comes from workers times threads, and I size with Little's law: in-flight equals throughput times latency."
3 · The hard part "Then memory, which is usually the real ceiling in AI backends. If each worker loads a two-gigabyte model, eight workers is sixteen gigabytes. I either preload before forking so pages are shared copy-on-write, with gc-freeze, or move the model to a separate inference service."
4 · Failure modes "Each symptom points at a different ceiling: OOM kills after scaling workers is model memory; too many connections is pool times workers times pods."
5 · What I'd monitor "Then I load-test at the target concurrency and watch CPU per worker, loop lag and p99. If CPU is low and latency is high, more workers won't help."
Close "Workers follow cores, threads follow in-flight I/O, and memory is the usual limit."

def in_flight(rps, latency_s): return rps * latency_s

python-q30.testing: that async concurrency outruns the pool, the multiplication across workers, and hold-time discipline.
python-q30.trap: growing the pool instead of shortening how long each request holds a connection.
python-q30.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the symptom "Async lets one worker accept hundreds of concurrent requests, but the pool might have ten connections. Everything beyond that queues at checkout. So the symptom is latency climbing under load while the database looks idle."
2 · Measure before guessing "So I measure checkout wait separately from query time. Tracing spans for acquire against execute make it obvious."
3 · Rank the suspects "The top suspect is a connection held across a slow await: a transaction opened at the start of the request stays open while the handler waits three seconds for an LLM. Second, the pool is per process, so real connections are pool times workers times pods."
4 · Confirm "To confirm, Postgres shows many sessions idle in transaction, and the pool's own status shows waiters."
5 · Fix "The fixes, in order: keep transactions narrow and never hold a connection across an external call; set a checkout timeout so overload fails fast; bound concurrency with a semaphore; and put PgBouncer in front when there are many pods. Growing the pool is last."
6 · Guard against the next one "And I guard it with pool metrics and a capacity formula in the deploy config."
Close "It's pool wait, not query time; shorten how long a connection is held."

stages.html:

p99 rises with concurrency; DB CPU and query latency are flat the wait is before the query
QueuePool limit of size 10 overflow 10 reached, or a timeout on acquire the pool is exhausted
After scaling out: FATAL: sorry, too many clients already pool × workers × pods exceeded the server limit

  • Errors like QueuePool limit of size 10 overflow 10 reached, connection timed out or TimeoutError on acquire.
  • After scaling out: FATAL: sorry, too many clients already.

stages.name: Measure before guessing
stages.html:
50 concurrent requests, pool of 5, each query 0.1 s
rounds = 50 / 5 = 10     → the last request waits 9 × 0.1 s = 0.9 s for a 0.1 s query
Time is spent Database sees
Waiting for a connection nothing: only 5 fast queries at a time

Prove it — 50 concurrent requests, a pool of 5 (simulated with a semaphore):

import asyncio, time
pool = asyncio.Semaphore(5)                     # stands in for a 5-connection pool
async def request():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    async with pool:                            # checkout
        wait = time.perf_counter() - t0
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)                # a 100 ms query
    return wait
async def main():
    waits = await asyncio.gather(*(request() for _ in range(50)))
    print(f"max wait {max(waits):.1f}s for a 0.1s query")
asyncio.run(main())
# → max wait 0.9s for a 0.1s query

The last requests wait 9 rounds of 0.1 s. The DB saw only 5 fast queries at a time.

3 pool × workers × pods > max_connections failures only after scaling out
4 Leaked connections on error paths (no context manager) in-use never falls

async def handle(q):
    async with Session() as s:                  # short: read what we need
        ctx = await load_context(s, q)
    answer = await llm.generate(ctx)            # no connection held here

  • A semaphore around DB work sized to the pool.
  • PgBouncer (transaction pooling) when pods × pools gets large; with asyncpg, disable its prepared-statement cache or use a PgBouncer version that supports prepared statements.

low load: fine      peak: "too many clients"

A bigger pool moves the queue into the database.

Fact Consequence
The database has a hard connection limit you can't grow far
Each connection costs it memory more is slower
Requests hold connections across slow awaits a bigger pool fills the same way

Shorten the hold time first.

A session opened a transaction and is doing something else.

In an async service, usually Side effects
an await on an external call inside a session block the connection is unavailable; locks are held; vacuum is blocked

followUps.html:
Multiplex, and keep each piece small.

Measure Effect

Small per-process pools, short transactions less held at once
Read replicas heavy reads off the primary

Unbounded waiting timeouts everywhere; memory piles up

"Increase the pool" as the first fix.
Holding a session across an LLM call.

python-q31.testing: the real-world problems — proxy buffering, disconnects, mid-stream errors — not just "use SSE."
python-q31.trap: assuming the upstream LLM call stops when the browser tab closes.
python-q31.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Constraints "Time to first token matters more than total time, streams last seconds to minutes with proxies in between, and every generated token costs money."
2 · Runtime model "For one-way token streaming I use Server-Sent Events: plain HTTP, text event-stream, one data line per event. In FastAPI it's a StreamingResponse over an async generator that reads the provider's stream. WebSockets only if I need two-way messaging."
3 · The hard part "The hard part is disconnects. If the user closes the tab, my generator must stop and the upstream call must be cancelled in a finally, or I keep paying for tokens nobody reads. Backpressure is natural with an async generator, as long as I don't put an unbounded queue in between."
4 · Failure modes "Then the failure modes. Proxies and compression buffer the response, so I send X-Accel-Buffering no. Load balancers cut idle streams, so I send heartbeats. And an error mid-stream can't become a 500, because the 200 is already sent: I send an in-band error event."
5 · What I'd monitor "I'd monitor time to first token, the client-abort rate, and tokens generated after a disconnect, which should be near zero."
Close "SSE over an async generator; cancel upstream on disconnect; errors travel in-band."

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html:
Constraint Consequence
Time to first token matters more than total time stream; nothing may buffer in between
Streams last seconds to minutes idle timeouts on proxies and load balancers apply
Every generated token costs money a stream nobody reads must be cancelled
  • Time to first token matters more than total time.
  • Streams last seconds to minutes; proxies and load balancers sit in between.
  • Every generated token costs money.

stages.name: Runtime model
stages.html:
Prove it — the SSE framing and a generator that cleans up on cancel:

import asyncio, json
async def fake_llm():
    try:
        for tok in ["Hel", "lo", "!"]:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.05); yield tok
    finally:
        print("upstream closed")               # where the provider stream is closed
async def sse():
    async for tok in fake_llm():
        yield f"data: {json.dumps({'t': tok})}\n\n"
    yield "event: done\ndata: {}\n\n"
async def main():
    async for frame in sse(): print(repr(frame))
asyncio.run(main())
# → 'data: {"t": "Hel"}\n\n' · 'data: {"t": "lo"}\n\n' · 'data: {"t": "!"}\n\n'   (one per line)
# → upstream closed
# → 'event: done\ndata: {}\n\n'

In FastAPI: return StreamingResponse(sse(), media_type="text/event-stream", headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"}).

Concern Mechanism Trap
Disconnect Starlette stops iterating; the task is cancelled; the generator's finally closes the provider stream (async with client.stream(...)) a detached task keeps generating
Long pauses between tokens (tool calls) also poll await request.is_disconnected() you only notice a disconnect when you try to send

Provider call runs After the tab closes

SSE WebSocket
Direction server → client both

Decouple the generation from the HTTP connection.

Flow:a generation idtokens persisted as produced (Redis Streams)the client reconnects with Last-Event-IDthe server replays from that offsetthe generation continues in a worker throughout

That also decouples billing from the connection.

Thousands, as far as the event loop is concerned.

Real limit Why
File descriptors one per connection
Memory per stream buffers, context
The provider's concurrency limits upstream
CPU for JSON encoding per token

Load-test with slow clients, not only fast ones.

python-q32.testing: a measurement-first habit and the right profiler for each situation.
python-q32.trap: micro-optimising a function that isn't at the top of the profile.
python-q32.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the symptom "First I pin down what slow means: which endpoint or job, which percentile, since when, and under what load. A p99 regression since yesterday's deploy is a different problem from a batch job that was always slow."
2 · Measure before guessing "Then I split wall-clock time into CPU against waiting. If a request takes two seconds and uses fifty milliseconds of CPU, profiling Python won't help: the time is in the database, a downstream call or a lock."
3 · Rank the suspects "And waiting is the usual cause in a service: N plus one queries, sequential awaits, pool wait."
4 · Confirm "If it is CPU, I pick the profiler for the situation. In production, py-spy: it attaches to a running process by PID with no restart, and gives a flame graph. Locally, cProfile with snakeviz. For line level, Scalene. For async, loop lag and traces."
5 · Fix "Then I fix only what's at the top of the profile, re-measure, and stop when the budget is met."
6 · Guard against the next one "And I guard it with latency SLOs, benchmarks on hot paths, and a continuous profiler."
Close "Define slow, split wall from CPU, then the right tool for that kind of slow."

python-q33.testing: criteria for queuing, and the delivery semantics that make consumers idempotent.
python-q33.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Constraints "I move work to a queue when it takes longer than the request's latency budget, when it must survive a crash and be retried, when the load is spiky, or when it needs different resources like a GPU."
2 · Runtime model "The API enqueues and returns a job id, and the client polls a status endpoint or gets a webhook. The worker acknowledges the message only after the effect is committed."
3 · The hard part "What breaks is delivery semantics. Queues deliver at least once: a worker can finish and crash before acknowledging, so the message comes again. Consumers must be idempotent: upsert by a business key, or record processed message ids in the same transaction as the effect."
4 · Failure modes "The other failures: a visibility timeout shorter than the real processing time hands a slow job to a second worker. And a poison message needs bounded retries with backoff, then a dead-letter queue with an alert."
5 · What I'd monitor "I'd monitor queue depth and the age of the oldest message, which is the real latency, plus the retry rate and the dead-letter size."
Close "At-least-once delivery, idempotent consumers, bounded retries, and a dead-letter queue."

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html:
Signal Example
longer than request budget ingesting and embedding a large document
must survive crashes, retryable sending emails, billing events
spiky load batch uploads at 9 a.m.
different resources GPU embedding, OCR
not a fit a 50 ms step the user waits for: do it inline or with a process pool

stages.name: Runtime model
The hard part
stages.html:
Delivery Message m1 processed table chunks rows
1st insert the id → do the work m1 1
2nd (redelivered) insert ignored: the id exists → skip m1 1

Prove it — the same message delivered twice, processed once:

import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE processed (msg_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE chunks (doc TEXT, n INT)")
def consume(msg_id, doc):
    with db:                                        # one transaction
        if db.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO processed VALUES (?)", (msg_id,)).rowcount == 0:
            return "duplicate, skipped"
        db.execute("INSERT INTO chunks VALUES (?, 42)", (doc,))
        return "processed"

1 · Constraints "I need one id to search by, timing per hop, and logs linked to the trace, across several services and a queue."
2 · Runtime model "I use OpenTelemetry. The first service starts a trace, or continues one from a traceparent header, the W3C standard. Every outbound call carries that header, and the receiver continues the same trace. Auto-instrumentation for FastAPI, httpx and SQLAlchemy does most of it, and each hop becomes a span."
3 · The hard part "The hard part is context across boundaries. Inside a Python service the current trace lives in contextvars: each Task gets a copy when it's created, so the trace follows awaits. Thread-locals don't, because every coroutine on the loop shares one thread. And run-in-executor doesn't copy context, while to-thread does."
4 · Failure modes "What breaks first is the queue hop: the worker starts a new trace unless I put the context into message headers. And log lines without trace ids."
5 · What I'd monitor "I'd monitor the share of traces that are complete end to end, and rate, errors and duration per service."

Prove it — contextvars follow tasks; plain executors don't:

import asyncio, contextvars
trace_id = contextvars.ContextVar("trace_id", default="-")
def read(): return trace_id.get()
async def aread(): return trace_id.get()
async def handler(tid):
    trace_id.set(tid)
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    a = await asyncio.to_thread(read)                  # copies the context
    b = await loop.run_in_executor(None, read)         # does not
    c = await asyncio.create_task(aread())            # tasks copy it
    return tid, a, b, c
async def main(): print(await asyncio.gather(handler("t1"), handler("t2")))
asyncio.run(main())
# → [('t1', 't1', '-', 't1'), ('t2', 't2', '-', 't2')]

Two concurrent requests keep separate IDs; the bare executor loses it.

Boundary What to do
HTTP out auto-instrument httpx/requests (injects traceparent)
queue inject context into message headers; extract in the consumer and start a linked span
thread pool asyncio.to_thread or contextvars.copy_context().run
fire-and-forget tasks created inside the request, so they inherit the context; make sure spans end

python-q35.testing: that you design for LLM-specific properties — slow, streaming, expensive, flaky, rate-limited — not a CRUD API.

python-q35.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Constraints "I start from what makes an LLM dependency different: calls take seconds, stream, cost money per token, fail or throttle often, and their output is untrusted."
2 · Runtime model "The service is async FastAPI end to end. At the edge: Pydantic validation, authentication, per-tenant rate limiting on requests and tokens, and an idempotency key for expensive non-streaming calls. The provider call goes through one shared async HTTP client, wrapped in a small gateway layer that owns reliability."
3 · The hard part "That gateway has timeouts, including time to first token; retries only on 429s and 5xx, with backoff and jitter, bounded to two or three attempts; a circuit breaker per provider; and a fallback model. And cost control is designed in: count input tokens before sending, cap max-tokens, cache where safe, and attribute usage per tenant."
4 · Failure modes "Each failure has a guard: a 429 storm, a hanging provider, retry amplification, a prompt that's too long, a client disconnect, and invalid output, which is validated before anything acts on it."
5 · What I'd monitor "For observability, beyond rate, errors and duration: time to first token, tokens in and out, cost per tenant, cache hit rate and fallback rate, all tagged with model and prompt version."
Close "Async edge, one gateway that owns reliability, and cost as a first-class limit."

Prove it — backoff with full jitter, bounded:

import random
rng = random.Random(0)                     # seeded for a repeatable demo
def backoff(attempt, base=0.5, cap=8.0):
    return rng.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt))
print([round(backoff(a), 2) for a in range(5)])

python-q36.testing: recognising two workload shapes in one process, and splitting them with batching and backpressure.
python-q36.trap: keeping both in one process and tuning worker counts forever.
python-q36.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Constraints "The service now has two workload shapes. The LLM proxy part is I/O-bound: async and lightweight. Embedding and reranking with local models are compute-bound, memory-heavy, and they want batches. In one process, inference blocks the event loop, and every API worker loads its own copy of the models."
2 · Runtime model "So I split them into two tiers. The API tier stays async and lean. Embedding and reranking move to an inference tier that loads each model once per process or per GPU. Online requests, like reranking the top fifty candidates, are a call with a tight timeout. Offline work, like embedding documents at ingestion, goes through a queue to batch workers."
3 · The hard part "Batching is where the performance comes from. Embedding one text at a time wastes the GPU. The inference server collects requests for a few milliseconds and runs them together; servers like TEI, Triton or vLLM do that for me."
4 · Failure modes "The root mistake is one process for both shapes. Others are an unbounded queue, and no timeout on the online rerank."
5 · What I'd monitor "I scale the tiers independently, and I watch batch sizes, GPU utilisation and queue depth, and that the API's p99 is unaffected by ingestion bursts."
Close "Two shapes, two tiers; batch the compute; scale each on its own signal."

stages.name: Runtime model
The hard part
stages.html:
40 concurrent embed() calls Model calls Batch sizes
One call per text 40 1 each
Micro-batcher (max_size=16, max_wait=10 ms) 3 16, 16, 8
Batcher loop:take the first itemwait up to max_wait for more, up to max_sizeone model callresolve each caller's future

Prove it — a micro-batcher: many concurrent callers, few model calls:

import asyncio
calls = []
def model(batch): calls.append(len(batch)); return [len(t) for t in batch]
class Batcher:
    def __init__(self, max_size=16, max_wait=0.01): self.q, self.n, self.w = asyncio.Queue(), max_size, max_wait
    async def embed(self, text):
        fut = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future(); await self.q.put((text, fut)); return await fut
    async def run(self):
        while True:
            items = [await self.q.get()]
            try:
                async with asyncio.timeout(self.w):
                    while len(items) < self.n: items.append(await self.q.get())
            except TimeoutError: pass
            for (_, f), r in zip(items, model([t for t, _ in items])): f.set_result(r)
async def main():
    b = Batcher(); asyncio.create_task(b.run())
    await asyncio.gather(*(b.embed("x" * i) for i in range(40))); print(calls)
asyncio.run(main())
# → [16, 16, 8]

40 requests became 3 model calls. In production the model call runs in a thread or on the GPU so the loop stays free.
